quietus.title: English Folk Dance and Song Society Changes Name
quietus.description: It marks a major shift as the organisation approaches its centenary Cecil Sharp House The English Folk Dance and Song Society has formally changed its trading name to Folk England, a decision it says aligns with a mission to "make folk music, song, and dance inclusive for all." Founded in 1932 following the merger of the Folk-Song Society and the English Folk Dance Society, the decision represents one of the biggest change in the organisation's history. Katy Spicer, Chief Executive & Artistic Director of Folk England, said of the decision: “For some years we have recognised that the breadth and ambition of the organisation’s work has far outgrown the confined and outdated previous name and…

quietus.title: Into The Risk Area: Factory Floor Interviewed
quietus.description: Jim Osman talks to a newly revitalised Factory Floor on the eve of the release of their first album in ten years, One Trip. All portraits: Harry Ward One Trip by Factory Floor What catches Nik Colk Void’s eye is not the dramatic landscape itself but evidence that somebody has been there before her: tape torn from a wall, scratches in a surface, cables worn through years of use. She finds a similar fascination in the photograph that graces the sleeve of One Trip, Factory Floor’s first album in ten years. Taken by their longtime associate Georg Gatsas, it presents the odd image of blocks of ice deposited on a road beside temporary emergency barriers. Something extreme has happened just…

quietus.title: 45 Years On: OMD’s Architecture & Morality Remembered
quietus.description: Orchestral Manoeuvres In The Dark released one of the Quietus' favourite albums in 1981. John Doran reflects on the warmth of Architecture & Morality and talks to Andy McCluskey A lazy but widespread criticism of the English synth pop scene of the early 80s was that it was soulless or lacking in human warmth. While there certainly were acts who came across as detached or alienated (Cabaret Voltaire, The Normal, John Foxx) if anything, the opposite was generally true. There is an almost baroque level of (exquisitely judged) romantic melodrama to Soft Cell's 'Say Hello Wave Goodbye'; despite Gary Numan's dead-eyed automaton image, Tubeway Army's 'Are "Friends" Electric?' is quite clearly a…

quietus.title: Reissue of the Week: Henning Christiansen’s Symphony Natura
quietus.description: Why Listen to Animals? asks Francis Gooding after immersing himself in some questionable musique concrète Symphony Natura by Henning Christiansen and Lorenzo Mammi "The zoo", wrote John Berger in a 1977 essay called 'Why Look At Animals?', "cannot but disappoint". The purpose of the visit is to see the animals, to look at them, but the animals always avoid being seen: they are bunched up at the edge of their enclosures, they are lethargic, they are hidden in their sleeping quarters, they are indifferent to the visitor. Berger was writing about the scopic regime of the zoological garden: it is a place where one goes to look at animals, and no matter the real or imagined conservation…

But it was the sounds of the evening, the music that sticks in my mind the most. My dear friend, the groom, arrived with noisy...

quietus.title: Tim Reaper’s Debut Solo Album Set for Release via Hyperdub
quietus.description: World's End is out in February Photo by Jimmy Mould Tim Reaper will release his debut solo album, World's End, via Hyperdub early next year. Featuring 11 tracks, the LP follows the jungle producer's previous collaborative album with Kloke, In Full Effect, which Hyperdub put out in 2024. In recent years, he's continued to put out EPs at a steady rate via labels such as FABRICLIVE, Rinse, Astrophonica and his own Future Retro London. World's End naturally explores various shades of jungle, as well as footwork, drill and gqom. The producer was inspired to fold other sub-genres into his sound after experimenting more on his 2024 EP Scorched Earth. In a statement, he said: "Scorched Earth EP…

quietus.title: Open Mind, Open Planet: Gigi Masin’s Favourite Albums
quietus.description: As his cult classic 1986 album Wind receives an expanded reissue, Italian composer and ambient pioneer Gigi Masin takes Siobhan Kane through his life in 13 records The renewed interest in Gigi Masin’s 1986 album Wind has taken the Venetian by surprise. He sees it as “strange and wonderful… I am really happy and honoured”. The expanded album, reissued by Numero Uno 40 years later, recontextualises Wind as an ambient gem, but an appreciation for Masin started some time ago, with artists such as Björk referencing his work, sampling ‘Clouds’ on her 2002 song ‘It’s In Our Hands’. Growing up in Italy, playing the guitar and working in radio, Masin was exposed to lots of different kinds of music,…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Dexter + Franz :: Panoramic Highway
aquariumdrunkard.description: While Panoramic Highway draws on a wide array of influences spanning geography and time, it's anchored by the sounds of Marin County’s coastline, where Dexter+Franz recorded at the Panoramic House. Throughout the album, field recordings and samples of the ocean and beaches seamlessly weave in and out of the songs. Waves crash, seagulls chirp, and synth textures float through the mix like gusts of salty sea breeze. In these moments, Panoramic Highway becomes an elemental experience, rooted in the soundscapes of nature.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Felt :: Be Still (The Beach Boys)
aquariumdrunkard.description: Toward the tail end of their ten-album run in the eighties, English jangle pop outfit Felt had sights on 1968's understated Beach Boys classic Friends for the band's only known cover. This transformative take on Dennis Wilson's soulful, momentary piano ballad "Be Still" sits comfortably next to Primal Scream's Screamadelica -era cover of another Dennis gem in "Carry Me Home" (keyboardist Martin Duffy would play in both bands). A shimmering beauty reminiscent of every frosty, ethereal component of the brilliance of Felt.

aquariumdrunkard.title: The Lagniappe Sessions :: Leah Senior
aquariumdrunkard.description: Australian singer-songwriter Leah Senior turns to two selections from the British folk guitar tradition for this installment of the Lagniappe Sessions. Recorded at home with Jesse Williams, her take on John Renbourn’s “Rainy Day” slows the tune’s insistent central riff, drawing out its sinuous, unhurried quality and the delicate, cascading descent that follows. On Jansch’s “Tell Me What Is True Love,” a lilting picking pattern opens onto a similarly pastoral expanse.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Kings of Convenience :: Quiet Is the New Loud
aquariumdrunkard.description: The muted hues, the subdued texture of the light, the encroaching dusk. There’s a sort of unspoken beautiful melancholy to autumn that has nothing to do with gloom or sadness. It hangs in the air, soft at the edges. Released 25 years ago this year, Kings of Convenience’s Quiet Is the New Loud gave that aching melancholy a voice.

This week on the show, we're digging into the work of Guaraldi with Peanuts historian and author of Vince Guaraldi at the Piano, Derrick Bang. We discuss it all: Guaraldi's fascination with the bossa nova sound in the late '50s, his status as a composer who didn't write or read music—writing from a purely melodic standpoint, his work with Brazilian guitarist Bola Sete; his groundbreaking Grace Cathedral Jazz Mass; and of course, his work on the animated Peanuts specials. If La Contra Ola crowned the industrial liturgies of Esplendor Geométrico and the electronic punk of Aviador Dro, and La Ola Interior drifted through the ambient, exotica, and proto-Balearic landscapes of Miguel A. Ruiz and post-minimalists like Javier Segura and Finis Africae, who carried the Fourth World Music of Jon Hassell and Brian Eno into Iberia, this new volume walks the borderlands between those territories, where left-field pop grew in parallel to unorthodox experiments, and in Madrid, but also in the smaller indie…
